title: Allen & Overy breaks the internet (and new ground) with co-pilot Harvey
author: Caroline Hill

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: Hill supports the cluster’s cautious Harvey test-case framing: she reports substantial law-firm deployment and workflow use while stressing unresolved reliability and verification risks and warning that firms may strengthen a future competitor. Her evidence supports early adoption and strategic pressure, not proven accuracy, autonomous matter delivery or durable vendor advantage.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: Hill’s report supports the cluster’s distinction between deployment volume and demonstrated value. It records substantial trial usage and firmwide rollout but provides no measured quality or productivity outcomes, treats efficiency benefits as attributed claims, and highlights that the response on error detection specifies no concrete verification process. Its report that rollout required little training is a limited counterpoint to the cluster’s emphasis on implementation support, not a rejection of the principal proposition.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that AI adoption can reshape legal work and competitive business models without establishing profession-wide displacement. It reinforces the need for verification and user expertise, while presenting reduced errors and serious competition from Harvey as conflicting, forward-looking claims rather than measured outcomes.

kp.k: Firmwide rollout follows substantial reported trial usage
kp.d: Caroline Hill reports that Allen & Overy rolled Harvey out across its 43 offices following a beta project led by its Markets Innovation Group, comprising lawyers and developers. Around 3,500 lawyers reportedly submitted around 40,000 queries for day-to-day client work by the trial's end. These are reported adoption figures, not measured accuracy or productivity results.
qs: The model, which has now been rolled out by A&O across its 43 offices, can automate various aspects of legal work, such as contract analysis, due diligence, litigation and regulatory compliance.
We’re told that at the end of the trial, around 3,500 of A&O’s lawyers had asked Harvey around 40,000 queries for their day-to-day client work.

kp.k: Legal specialisation builds on a general language model
kp.d: Hill describes Harvey as a legally specialised OpenAI model, cautiously identifying its underlying technology as what she understands to be GPT-4. She reports additional legal-sector training, $5m of OpenAI investment in November of the previous year, and beta work with several law firms. The model identification and training description are the author's account, not independently demonstrated technical findings.
qs: Harvey is a verticalised version of what I understand to be GPT-4, which has been trained on the entire corpus of the internet.
By verticalised, I mean that Harvey has further trained the model with legal sector-specific data.
Harvey, which in November last year received $5m in investment from OpenAI, has been working with a number of law firms – including A&O – in beta.

kp.k: Research and drafting become natural-language assisted workflows
kp.d: The article describes background research, first-pass drafting and legal-document generation as uses of Harvey, alongside contract analysis, due diligence, litigation and regulatory compliance. A&O claims faster, smarter and more cost-effective client services; MIG head David Wakeling also claims multilingual and cross-practice capabilities. These are reported capabilities and anticipated benefits rather than quantified efficiency findings.
qs: Harvey can be used for any sort of background research and first pass drafts.
Harvey is integrated into A&O’s legal workflows and is able to generate legal documents, not just text.
Harvey can work in multiple languages and across diverse practice areas, delivering unprecedented efficiency and intelligence.

It can generate insights, recommendations and predictions without requiring any immediate training, which A&O says will enable its lawyers to deliver faster, smarter and more cost-effective solutions to their clients.

kp.k: A&O claims minimal onboarding lowers deployment barriers
kp.d: Hill contrasts Harvey with earlier AI-based legal technologies requiring more work to deploy. An A&O spokesperson claims that a short list of parameters and tips replaces substantial user training, making rollout quick and inexpensive. The article provides no measured implementation costs or training outcomes.
qs: Harvey – unlike most AI-based legal technology offerings to date – really doesn’t require a lot of work to get it live.

One of the brilliant things about Harvey is that you don’t need to train people to use it; you just need to provide them with a short, simple list of parameters and tips (which we’ve done). So it’s quick, pain-free, and inexpensive to roll-out.

kp.k: Deployment depends on lawyers verifying every output
kp.d: A&O presents Harvey as a copilot, not a replacement for professional review. Its spokesperson promises lawyer review of all output and cites model-level safeguards, while also asserting that legal prompts make errors inherently less problematic than in other domains. Hill separately reports an FT account of a licensed-professional-supervision disclaimer and continuing hallucinations; the article supplies no measured error rate.
qs: There are safeguards in place at the model level, which will continue to improve over time and, the subject matter itself (i.e. legal) is one where this is inherently less of an issue than in other domains due to the nature of what will be prompted.
Importantly, there will be a lawyer in the loop reviewing all output to screen for this.

As reported by the FT, the AI assistant comes with a disclaimer that its use should be supervised by licensed legal professionals, and it does still “hallucinate”, which is when the programme can produce inaccurate or misleading results.

kp.k: Client confidentiality limits use of client data
kp.d: Hill reads A&O's press release as suggesting potential client-data use and raises concerns because clients had not been formally consulted. A&O's spokesperson instead states that Harvey will not interact with client data until safety is established, citing confidentiality protections and regular client contact. The spokesperson treats formal consultation as unnecessary for an internal tool; Hill disputes the analogy to ordinary tools. Actual safe client-data deployment is not established.
qs: Sharing client data with Harvey would be problematic for a number of reasons, not least because A&O hasn’t formally consulted clients.
Harvey is designed for the legal industry and as a result has myriad ways to ensure client confidentiality. Harvey will not interact with client data until we know it is safe to do so.
The spokesperson added that A&O is in regular contact with its clients, they just haven’t done a formal consultation, as they wouldn’t with any new tool they start using internally.
But Harvey is not just any new tool.

kp.k: Fluent fabrication threatens the effectiveness of human verification
kp.d: Radiant Law founder Alex Hamilton argues that fabricated content, opaque workings and absent confidence levels combine with fluent presentation to encourage unwarranted trust. He identifies human weaknesses in checking plausible material and noticing omissions, citing checklists as important. An anonymous Am Law top 100 CIO similarly argues that deployment and user behaviour matter, particularly when users lack the knowledge needed to recognise errors.
qs: The underlying technology is prone to hallucinations (aka making stuff up, not just being wildly wrong); does not show its workings (it’s a black box); does not show its confidence levels; and lulls people into a false sense of security by answering fluently.
We are then up against very human problems of being a) bad at checking things that seem fine and b) not noticing things that are missing, which is why checklists are such an important tool.
But if the user doesn’t know what they don’t know, it will be really hard to tell that what the machine says is trash.

kp.d: An anonymous UK top 50 firm CTO warns that juniors may miss consequential errors and predicts that solving accuracy is a five-to-ten-year problem. Investor Zach Abramowitz counters that juniors already miss things and will miss fewer with the technology. These opposing predictions are not supported by comparative junior-lawyer performance measurements in the article.
qs: The accuracy problem is a five-to-ten-year problem, and I don’t know how they have sorted that out in a few months.
It has the potential to cause damage when some poor junior lawyer misses the fact of the case.
Junior lawyers miss things every day. They will miss less now.

kp.k: Training AI may erode firms' competitive advantage
kp.d: Hill argues that A&O is helping train a model that will become a serious competitor. The anonymous UK top 50 CTO develops this concern into a prediction that law-firm-assisted improvements will drive the cost of intelligence to zero and undermine firms' competitive edge. This is a speculative market-disruption argument, not evidence of realised displacement or price reductions.
qs: While the magic circle firm is being progressive and leading the market, it is also helping to train a model that will become a serious competitor.

In a move to become progressive are they not giving away their competitive edge? The accuracy of the AI will improve – helped by law firms training it – and the cost of intelligence will turn to zero. The rush to be innovative will be our downfall.

kp.k: Client adoption could make generative AI commercially necessary
kp.d: Abramowitz counters competitive-threat concerns by likening GPT to the iPhone and predicting that clients' own use will create pressure for law firms to adopt it. His distinction is between specialist tools clients would not ordinarily demand and broadly accessible technology clients may expect their lawyers to use.
qs: GPT isn’t like anything we’ve seen in the past, it’s more akin to the introduction of the iPhone. Clients will be using it themselves.
They wouldn’t come to a law firm and say, ‘Why on earth aren’t you using this particular eDiscovery tool?’ but they will start coming to legal and saying, ‘why are you not using ChatGPT?’

kp.k: Further firm adoption and model competition are anticipated
kp.d: Hill predicts further law-firm announcements and reports that Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan is among other firms working with Harvey. Professor Daniel Katz predicts many competing large language models within 12 months, probably sooner, and expects discussion to extend beyond GPT by the end of 2023. Hill notes Google's subsequent Bard announcement, but leaves consequences for existing legal-technology providers unresolved.
qs: Other firms reported to be working with Harvey include Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan.

In the next 12 months, probably less than 12 months, there will be many other large language models in a competitive market. So GPT will not be the only thing we’re talking about by the end of this year.
Within days of that conversation, Google announced the launch of its GPT rival Bard.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harvey can automate parts of legal work and assist research and drafting; A&O claims this will improve speed, intelligence and cost-effectiveness.
pts.d: Caroline Hill reports capabilities spanning contract analysis, due diligence, litigation, regulatory compliance, background research and first-pass drafting, including generating legal documents within A&O workflows. A&O attributes faster, smarter and more cost-effective client service to these capabilities. MIG head David Wakeling predicts industry transformation and claims efficiency across languages and practice areas. These are augmentation claims: A&O requires lawyer review rather than direct reliance on autonomous output.

pts.k: An A&O spokesperson claims Harvey is quick and inexpensive to deploy, requiring little user training.
pts.d: Hill contrasts Harvey with earlier AI-based legal technology requiring substantial implementation work. The spokesperson says short parameters and tips suffice for users. This is a deployment and usability claim, distinct from proving that users can reliably verify its output.

pts.k: Interviewees disagree over whether AI assistance will increase missed errors or help junior lawyers miss fewer things.
pts.d: Alex Hamilton of Radiant Law argues that fabrication, opacity, absent confidence levels and fluent answers create false reassurance, compounded by human weaknesses in checking and spotting omissions. An anonymous Am Law top 100 CIO identifies blind trust and insufficient user knowledge as operational risks. An anonymous UK top 50 CTO predicts possible damage when junior lawyers miss case facts. Zach Abramowitz counters that junior lawyers already miss things and will miss fewer with AI. The document presents these as competing claims, not a measured comparison.

pts.k: Hill and an anonymous CTO foresee AI becoming a competitor to law firms; Abramowitz instead stresses client-driven pressure to adopt it.
pts.d: Hill argues that A&O is helping train a model that will become a serious competitor. The UK top 50 CTO predicts that law-firm training will improve AI accuracy, push the cost of intelligence to zero and undermine firms’ competitive advantage. Abramowitz predicts clients will use the technology themselves and question firms that do not. These are market forecasts without specified economic measurements or a firm deadline.

pts.k: Hill predicts wider law-firm adoption, while Daniel Katz predicts a competitive market of multiple large language models during 2023.
pts.d: Hill states that other firms will announce generative-AI incorporation and reports Quinn Emanuel among firms working with Harvey. Katz predicts many competing models within twelve months, probably sooner, so discussion will no longer centre only on GPT by the end of 2023. Hill points to Google's subsequent Bard announcement. The article explicitly leaves the impact on existing legal-technology providers for another discussion.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The adoption and benefit claims rest on reported trial usage, A&O testimony and illustrative prompts, not quantified quality or productivity results.
pts.d: Hill reports approximately 3,500 lawyers and 40,000 queries during the beta trial, followed by deployment across 43 offices. Wakeling invokes fifteen years of legal-technology experience and favourable trial results, but no accuracy scores, time savings, cost comparisons or controlled evaluations are supplied. Example prompts illustrate proposed research and drafting uses rather than demonstrate answer quality. The spokesperson's claims about easy rollout, safeguards and confidentiality are institutional assurances.

pts.k: Risk and competitive forecasts are principally expert opinion; the article offers no measured hallucination rate or economic displacement evidence.
pts.d: Hill states that OpenAI's model has produced confidently wrong answers and cites FT reporting of Harvey's supervision disclaimer and continuing hallucinations, without presenting specific test results or incidents. Hamilton and anonymous technology executives supply explanations of error and verification risks; Abramowitz supplies a counterprediction. The competitive-threat and client-pressure arguments have no supporting market data in the document. Katz's model-competition forecast is accompanied by the concrete Bard announcement, while wider firm adoption is supported by reported work with Quinn Emanuel.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported rollout is current to February 2023, with lawyer verification and safe handling of client data as explicit conditions.
pts.d: The article describes an already-completed beta and rollout. A&O says all output will be reviewed by a lawyer and model safeguards will improve over time; its spokesperson additionally asserts that legal prompts make errors inherently less of an issue than in other domains. Although the press release prompted questions about client-data use, the spokesperson says Harvey will not interact with client data until safety is established. Hill reports no formal client consultation. These qualifications limit any inference that all advertised data-intensive capabilities were already operating on confidential client material.

pts.k: Forecast horizons differ: one CTO places the accuracy problem at five to ten years, while Katz expects model competition within 2023.
pts.d: The anonymous UK top 50 CTO characterises resolving accuracy as a five-to-ten-year problem, questioning whether a few months could suffice. Katz forecasts competing models within twelve months of his February 2023 interview, probably sooner, and explicitly by year-end. Abramowitz's claim that juniors will miss fewer things is immediate in phrasing. Broader predictions about client adoption, competitors to firms and zero-cost intelligence carry no precise deadline; the CIO makes beneficial deployment conditional on preventing blind trust.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central affected groups are large law firms, their lawyers—particularly juniors—and their clients, with wider implications for model suppliers.
pts.d: A&O lawyers across 43 offices are the immediate users, gaining research and drafting assistance while retaining verification responsibility. Junior lawyers are singled out both as vulnerable to missed AI errors and as potential beneficiaries of reduced omissions. Clients are promised faster, smarter, lower-cost service, but face confidentiality concerns and may become direct users who pressure firms to adopt AI. A&O and other firms face predicted erosion of competitive advantage alongside pressure to innovate. Model suppliers face predicted competition. No concrete access-to-justice, staffing-reduction or existing legal-tech-provider impact is established or forecast in detail.
